# Tittirajātaka (Ja 37)

**ID:** Ja 37
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Tittirajātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Tittirajātaka* (Ja 37) is a short moral fable in the Pali Jātaka collection emphasizing respect for elders and mutual cooperation [Beer 1999; Anandajoti 2010]. In its narrative setting (*paccuppannavatthu*), while travelling to Sāvatthī, the elder Sāriputta was left without a night's lodging and forced to sleep beneath a tree or a shelter of robes because younger monks had hurried ahead to secure all available accommodations for themselves [Beer 1999; Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. To counter this lack of deference, the Buddha related the tale of three animal friends—an elephant, a monkey, and a partridge—dwelling together beneath a great banyan tree in the Himalayan foothills [Beer 1999; Anandajoti 2010]. When their mutual respect diminished, they determined their relative seniority by recounting how small the banyan tree had been when they first encountered it; discovering the partridge to be the oldest, the monkey and elephant rendered him homage and accepted his moral instruction [Beer 1999; Anandajoti 2010; Horner 1952]. Living in accordance with the five moral precepts, this practice became known as the "Partridge Brahma-faring" (*tittira-brahmacariya*), culminating in the Buddha's promulgation of the rule that monastic quarters must be allocated strictly by seniority [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Horner 1952]. The moral verse underscores that those who honor the aged and are skilled in the Dhamma are praised in this life and destined for a happy bourn hereafter (*Ye vuddham-apacāyanti narā Dhammassa kovidā*) [Anandajoti 2010; Horner 1952].

This narrative represents one of the Jātaka stories embedded directly within the canonical Vinaya Piṭaka, occurring in the *Senāsanakkhandhaka* of the *Cullavagga* (VI.6.3 / Kd 16) [Clark 1994; Horner 1952]. Comparable versions of the account appear across other early Buddhist Vinaya traditions, including the Mahīśāsaka, Dharmaguptaka, and Mahāsāṃghika Vinayas [Dhammajoti 1995]. Parallel or resembling verses are found in Sanskrit and Chinese collections such as the *Udānavarga* (UV 5, UVS 5, T 212, T 213) and within the Jātaka corpus itself in the *Vighāsādajātaka* (Ja 393), though DharmaNexus detected no automated cross-language matches meeting its threshold [DharmaNexus]. The story is carefully distinguished in modern scholarship from other homonymous tales, such as the *Tittira Jātaka* (Ja 319) concerning a decoy bird [Crosby 2014]. Beyond the textual canon, this fable provided the foundation for the prominent Buddhist and Tibetan cultural motif of the "four friends" beneath a tree, illustrating cooperation and reverence for age [Beer 1999].
